title: A Personal History in Quantum Foundations: an Oral History Interview
abstract: This oral history interview provides Yakir Aharonov's personal and conceptual recollections from the 1950s to the 2000s, focusing on his academic trajectory, some of his major contributions to quantum foundations, and his perspective on the development of the field. The interview traces Aharonov's academic career through the Technion, University of Bristol, Brandeis University, Yeshiva University, University of South Carolina, Tel Aviv University, George Mason University, and Chapman University. The interview also traces the development of Aharonov's work and collaborations on the EPR paradox, time-energy uncertainty relations, quantum measurement theory, quantum frames of reference, the two-state vector formalism, weak values, protective measurements, and several other contributions. It includes recollections of meetings and discussions with David Bohm, Niels Bohr, John Clauser, Paul Dirac, Rudolf Peierls, Aage Petersen, and Abner Shimony. Also mentioned: David Albert, Jeeva Anandan, Peter Bergmann, Gideon Carmi, Avshalom Elitzur, Dave Finkelstein, Vladimir Fock, Itzhak Kalugai, Ed Lerner, Joel Lebowitz, Stanley Mandelstam, Yuval Ne'eman, Sandu Popescu, Maurice Pryce, Daniel Rohrlich, Nathan Rosen, Joseph Safko, Paul Singer, Daniele Struppa, Leonard Susskind, Lev Vaidman, Chien-Shiung Wu.
summary: This paper is an oral history interview detailing the conceptual evolution of quantum foundations, covering topics from the EPR paradox to modern weak measurements. It synthesizes complex theoretical developments, such as the two-state-vector formalism, to clarify how quantum mechanics describes reality beyond classical intuition. It is essential reading for understanding the theoretical underpinnings of quantum measurement and correlation.
main_problem: The paper reviews the conceptual development of quantum foundations, focusing on resolving paradoxes like the EPR paradox and understanding measurement processes.
main_result: It details advanced formalisms like the two-state-vector formalism and protective measurements, demonstrating how quantum correlations exceed classical limits.
method: The discussion is historical and conceptual, synthesizing results from various theoretical calculations and thought experiments.
model_or_system: The discussion covers general quantum mechanics principles, including positronium decay, quantum random walks, and the separation of physical attributes like spin from particle location.
key_observables: Polarization correlations of photons, energy/momentum measurements over short times, and weak values.
important_parameters: Time intervals ($\Delta t$), measurement strength, and the number of particles/holes in combinatorial examples.
main_assumptions: The analysis often contrasts the Schrödinger picture with the Heisenberg picture to resolve conceptual contradictions in quantum description.
paper_structure: The structure follows a historical narrative, moving from early tests of quantum correlations (EPR, positronium decay) to modern formalisms (TSVF, protective measurements) and conceptual debates (Heisenberg vs. Schrödinger pictures).
why_interesting: It provides deep historical context and advanced theoretical tools (like weak measurements and TSVF) crucial for understanding open quantum systems and measurement theory, which are foundational to AMO physics.
